L107@P1: Here we assess this possibility by taking the study of
L108@P1: change blindness into the real world. Rather than changing
L109@P1: the sole actor in a video, we changed the subjects’ conversation partner during a typical daily interaction.
L110@P1: EXPERIMENT 1
L111@P1: In Experiment 1, we created a situation that allowed us
L112@P1: to surreptitiously substitute one individual for another in
L113@P1: the middle of a natural, real-world interaction. The situation we chose was asking directions of a pedestrian on
L114@P1: a college campus.1 We temporarily interrupted this interaction by carrying a door between the experimenter and
L115@P1: the pedestrian. While the experimenter was occluded by
L116@P1: the door, another experimenter took his place and continued the interaction after the door had passed. If changedetection failures are based on the passive nature of mediated stimuli, these substitutions should be clearly
L117@P1: detectable.
L118@P1: Method
L119@P1: Subjects. A total of 15 pedestrians were approached on the campus
L120@P1: of Cornell University. They ranged in approximate age from 20 to 65.
L121@P1: Only pedestrians walking alone or together with one other person (two
L122@P1: cases) were approached.
L123@P1: Procedure. An experimenter carrying a campus map asked unsuspecting pedestrians for directions to a nearby building (see Figure 1a).
L124@P1: Pedestrians had a clear view of the experimenter starting from a distance of approximately 20 m as they walked down a sidewalk. After the
L125@P1: experimenter and pedestrian had been talking for 10–15 sec, two other
L126@P1: experimenters carrying a door rudely passed between them. As the door
L127@P1: passed, the first experimenter grabbed the back of the door, and the experimenter who had been carrying that part of the door stayed behind
L128@P1: and continued to ask for directions (Figure 1c). The first experimenter
L129@P1: kept his map during the interruption, and the second experimenter produced an identical copy of the map after the door passed. The door
L130@P1: blocked the pedestrian’s view for approximately 1 sec (Figure 1b). From
L131@P1: the subject’s perspective, the door briefly occluded his/her conversation
L132@P1: partner, and when it was gone, a different person was revealed. As the
L133@P1: door passed, subjects typically made eye contact with the second experimenter before continuing to give directions.2 The entire interaction
L134@P1: took 2–5 min. The two experimenters wore different clothing and differed in height by approximately 5 cm (Figure 1d). Their voices were
L135@P1: also clearly distinguishable.
L136@P1: After a pedestrian finished giving directions, the experimenter told
L137@P1: him/her, “We’re doing a study as part of the psychology department [experimenter points to the psychology building next door] of the sorts of
L138@P1: things people pay attention to in the real world. Did you notice anything
L139@P1-2: unusual at all when that door passed by a minute ago?” Responses were646 SIMONS AND LEVIN
L140@P2: noted by the experimenter, and if subjects failed to report the change,
L141@P2: they were directly asked, “Did you notice that I’m not the same person
L142@P2: who approached you to ask for directions?” After answering this question, all subjects were informed about the purpose of the experiment.
L143@P2: Results and Discussion
L144@P2: If change blindness results from the passive nature of
L145@P2: mediated stimuli, then these real-world substitutions
L146@P2: should be detected. When asked if they had noticed anything unusual, most pedestrians reported that the people
L147@P2: carrying the door were rude. Yet, despite clear differences
L148@P2: in clothing, appearance, and voice, only 7 of the 15 pedestrians reported noticing the change of experimenters.
L149@P2: Those who did not notice the change continued the conversation as if nothing had happened (in fact, some
L150@P2: pedestrians who did notice the change also continued the
L151@P2: conversation!). Pedestrians who did not notice the change
L152@P2: were quite surprised to learn that the person standing in
L153@P2: front of them was different from the one who initiated
L154@P2: the conversation. One pedestrian who reported noticing
L155@P2: nothing unusual nonetheless claimed to have noticed the
L156@P2: change when asked directly.
L157@P2: Interestingly, those who noticed the change were all
L158@P2: students of roughly the same age as the experimenters
L159@P2: (approximately 20–30 years old). Those who failed to
L160@P2: detect the change were slightly older than the experimenters (approximately 35–65 years old). One possible
L161@P2: explanation for this difference is that younger pedestrians were more likely to expend effort encoding those
L162@P2: features that would differentiate the experimenters because the experimenters were roughly of their own generation. In contrast, older pedestrians would likely encode the experimenters without focusing on features that
L163@P2: could differentiate the two of them, instead viewing them
L164@P2: as members of a social group other than their own. This
L165@P2: hypothesis draws on findings from social psychology
